title: The Citric Acid Cycle: Harvesting Electrons

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Per acetyl-CoA, the citric acid cycle's real product is electrons, loaded onto {{c1::3 NADH and 1 FADH₂}} and shipped to the electron transport chain.
cards.back: Not ATP: the carriers go to the ETC, where the bulk of the ATP is made.
cards.quote: Its real product is electrons, loaded onto three NADH and one FADH₂ and shipped to the electron transport chain, where the bulk of your ATP is made.
cards.section: Where we are, and what the cycle is for

cards.front: How many high-energy phosphates does one turn of the citric acid cycle make directly, and in what form?
cards.back: Exactly one: a GTP (or ATP, depending on the succinyl-CoA synthetase isoform).
cards.quote: It is not: per turn it makes exactly one high-energy phosphate, a GTP.
cards.section: Where we are, and what the cycle is for

cards.front: Why is the cycle's single GTP a byproduct rather than the point of the cycle?
cards.back: One NADH's electron pair, handed to oxygen, releases about 220 kJ/mol; the GTP is worth about 30. Three NADH per turn dwarf one GTP.
cards.why: The cycle harvests electrons; the ETC spends them.
cards.quote: One NADH's electron pair, handed to oxygen, releases about 220 kJ/mol; the GTP is worth about 30.
cards.section: Where we are, and what the cycle is for

cards.front: Carbon in CO₂ is at oxidation state +4. In an acetyl group the methyl carbon is at −3 and the carbonyl carbon at +3. How many electrons must come off to make both into CO₂, and how many dehydrogenases (one pair each) does that predict?
cards.back: Methyl: −3 to +4 = 7; carbonyl: +3 to +4 = 1; total 8 electrons = 4 pairs, so 4 dehydrogenases (steps 3, 4, 6 and 8), giving 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂.
cards.quote: Eight electrons: 7 from the methyl carbon (−3 to +4) and 1 from the carbonyl carbon (+3 to +4).
cards.section: Where we are, and what the cycle is for

cards.front: In a respiring cell, why can the citric acid cycle turn no faster than the electron transport chain?
cards.back: Carriers must be emptied before they can be loaded again, and the ETC (ultimately oxygen) is what empties NADH and FADH₂.
cards.quote: Carriers must be emptied before they can be loaded again, so, in a respiring cell, the cycle can turn no faster than the electron transport chain
cards.section: Where we are, and what the cycle is for

cards.front: Citrate synthase joins 4-carbon oxaloacetate to 2-carbon acetyl-CoA, making {{c1::6-carbon citrate}}.
cards.back: Step 1, the condensation that starts each turn.
cards.quote: Citrate synthase joins 4-carbon oxaloacetate (OAA) to 2-carbon acetyl-CoA, making 6-carbon citrate.
cards.section: Stage One: the carbons leave (steps 1–4)

cards.front: Citrate synthase spends no ATP. Where does the energy for the condensation come from?
cards.back: From cleaving acetyl-CoA's high-energy thioester. A synthase uses no nucleotide triphosphate.
cards.quote: A synthase uses no ATP; the energy comes from cleaving acetyl-CoA's high-energy thioester.
cards.section: Stage One: the carbons leave (steps 1–4)

cards.front: Citrate already has an –OH. Why must aconitase convert it to isocitrate before it can be oxidized?
cards.back: Citrate's –OH is on a carbon with no hydrogen (a tertiary alcohol), so C–OH cannot become C=O without breaking a C–C bond. Aconitase moves the –OH to a carbon that has a hydrogen.
cards.quote: Citrate's –OH sits on a carbon with no hydrogen (a tertiary alcohol).
cards.section: Stage One: the carbons leave (steps 1–4)

cards.front: What is an oxidative decarboxylation, and which two citric acid cycle steps carry one out?
cards.back: Oxidize the substrate, then remove a carboxyl as CO₂. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (step 3) and the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (step 4), each yielding one CO₂ and one NADH.
cards.quote: Isocitrate dehydrogenase carries out the first oxidative decarboxylation: oxidize, then remove a carboxyl as CO₂.
cards.section: Stage One: the carbons leave (steps 1–4)

cards.front: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is often called the citric acid cycle's rate-limiting step. How does control actually work in living tissue?
cards.back: That is the answer exams usually expect, but in living tissue control is shared with citrate synthase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
cards.quote: In living tissue, control is shared with citrate synthase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
cards.section: Stage One: the carbons leave (steps 1–4)

cards.front: Succinyl-CoA synthetase (step 5) is the citric acid cycle's only {{c1::substrate-level phosphorylation}}.
cards.back: Cleaving succinyl-CoA's thioester drives GDP to GTP (or ADP to ATP).
cards.quote: Succinyl-CoA synthetase is the cycle's only substrate-level phosphorylation, a phosphate made directly by the reaction rather than by the chain.
cards.section: Stage Two: oxaloacetate is rebuilt (steps 5–8)

cards.front: Which citric acid cycle enzyme is membrane-bound, and what else is it?
cards.back: Succinate dehydrogenase (step 6). It sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is Complex II of the ETC, feeding electrons straight into the chain.
cards.quote: It sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is Complex II of the ETC, feeding electrons straight into the chain.
cards.section: Stage Two: oxaloacetate is rebuilt (steps 5–8)

cards.front: Succinate dehydrogenase takes two hydrogens off succinate's CH₂–CH₂. Why does the pair go to FAD rather than NAD⁺?
cards.back: Those electrons are too low in energy to reduce NAD⁺ (that would cost about 68 kJ/mol under standard conditions). The enzyme-bound FAD sits at a far more positive potential, so accepting them costs little.
cards.quote: Those electrons are too low in energy to reduce NAD⁺: handing them to NAD⁺ would cost about 68 kJ/mol under standard conditions.
cards.section: Stage Two: oxaloacetate is rebuilt (steps 5–8)

cards.front: Fumarase adds water across fumarate's double bond to make {{c1::L-malate}}.
cards.back: Step 7, a stereospecific hydration.
cards.quote: Fumarase adds water across fumarate's double bond to make L-malate.
cards.section: Stage Two: oxaloacetate is rebuilt (steps 5–8)

cards.front: The malate dehydrogenase step (malate to oxaloacetate) is unfavorable on its own. Why does it still run forward in the cycle?
cards.back: Citrate synthase uses up oxaloacetate the instant it appears, pulling step 8 forward. The steps are coupled, not independent.
cards.quote: This step is unfavorable on its own, but citrate synthase uses up OAA the instant it appears, pulling it forward.
cards.section: Stage Two: oxaloacetate is rebuilt (steps 5–8)

cards.front: Malonate (succinate minus one CH₂) is added to respiring mitochondria. Predict which citric acid cycle intermediates rise and which fall.
cards.back: Succinate accumulates; fumarate, malate and oxaloacetate are depleted.
cards.why: Malonate competitively inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, so its substrate backs up and everything downstream runs dry: a traffic jam.
cards.quote: Competitively inhibited by malonate (succinate minus one CH₂), a classic traffic jam.

cards.front: Fluoroacetate is converted in cells to fluorocitrate, which jams aconitase. Predict the effect on citrate levels and on NADH output from the cycle.
cards.back: Citrate backs up; isocitrate is not made, so steps 3, 4 and onward lose substrate and the cycle's NADH (and FADH₂) output falls.
cards.why: Rests on the substrate-backup logic of an inhibited step.
cards.quote: a suicide inhibitor that jams aconitase and backs up citrate

cards.front: Citrate synthase is selectively inhibited in isolated mitochondria. Predict what happens at the malate dehydrogenase step and to NADH #3.
cards.back: Step 8 stalls: oxaloacetate is no longer drawn off, so the step loses the pull that makes it run forward, and NADH #3 is no longer made.
cards.why: Rests on the coupling rule: step 8 runs forward only because step 1 consumes oxaloacetate.
cards.quote: In isolation this step is strongly unfavorable (very positive ΔG°′), but citrate synthase immediately consumes oxaloacetate, pulling it forward

cards.front: Why does oxaloacetate cancel out of the net equation for one turn of the citric acid cycle, and what does that imply?
cards.back: One OAA goes in at step 1 and one comes out at step 8. It is reusable, not fuel, so a small pool supports many turns; the fuel is acetyl-CoA.
cards.quote: One OAA goes in at step 1 and one comes out at step 8, so OAA appears on both sides and cancels
cards.section: Add it up: oxaloacetate cancels

cards.front: A pinch of a four-carbon acid added to minced pigeon breast muscle makes the muscle burn far more oxygen than oxidizing that pinch could explain. What does this show?
cards.back: The acid is not consumed as fuel. It joins the pool of four-carbon intermediates and is handed back each turn, so each molecule carries many acetyl groups through, each sending electrons to oxygen.
cards.quote: Add a pinch of a four-carbon acid to minced pigeon breast muscle, and the muscle burns far more oxygen than oxidizing that pinch could ever explain.

cards.front: Counting only the citric acid cycle itself, how many NADH, FADH₂, GTP and CO₂ come from one glucose?
cards.back: One glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA = 2 turns. 2 × (3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂) = 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 GTP, 4 CO₂.
cards.quote: One glucose, two acetyl-CoA, two turns of the cycle.
cards.section: Where we are, and what the cycle is for

cards.front: Acetyl-CoA labeled at both acetyl carbons enters the citric acid cycle, and exactly one turn finishes. Is any label released as CO₂?
cards.back: None. Both CO₂ of that turn come from oxaloacetate-derived carbons; the labeled acetyl carbons stay in the four-carbon intermediates.
cards.why: Steps 3 and 4 remove carboxyls on the OAA-derived arm of citrate, which aconitase selects.
cards.quote: The orange carbons are untouched in the first turn. The atoms that leave are older ones.
cards.section: Which carbons leave? A puzzle the net equation cannot answer

cards.front: Citrate's two CH₂–COO⁻ arms look identical on paper. How can aconitase act on only one of them?
cards.back: The arms sit in mirror-image positions around the central carbon. An enzyme that grips citrate at three points holds it in only one orientation, like a right glove on one hand.
cards.quote: so an enzyme that grips citrate at three points holds it in only one orientation, the way a right glove fits only one hand.
cards.section: Which carbons leave? A puzzle the net equation cannot answer

cards.front: Why does carbon tracking in the citric acid cycle become a matter of odds from succinate onward?
cards.back: Succinate (⁻OOC–CH₂–CH₂–COO⁻) reads the same from either end, so no enzyme can tell its ends apart. Fumarate is symmetric too.
cards.quote: At step 5 the chain becomes succinate, ⁻OOC–CH₂–CH₂–COO⁻, which reads the same from either end, so no enzyme can tell the ends apart.
cards.section: Which carbons leave? A puzzle the net equation cannot answer

cards.front: Acetyl-CoA labeled only at the methyl carbon enters the citric acid cycle. The share released as CO₂ is 0 in turn 1, 0 in turn 2, ½ in turn 3 and ¼ in turn 4. What fraction of the label is still in intermediates after four turns?
cards.back: 1 − 0 − 0 − ½ − ¼ = ¼. Each later turn releases half of what remains.
cards.why: The methyl becomes a middle carbon, and each turn moves a middle carbon to an end only half the time.
cards.quote: The methyl carbon lingers because a middle carbon must first be moved to an end, and each turn does that only half the time.
cards.section: Which carbons leave? A puzzle the net equation cannot answer

cards.front: Acetyl-CoA labeled only at the carbonyl carbon enters the citric acid cycle. In which turn is the label released as CO₂, and how much of it?
cards.back: All of it, in turn 2. After turn 1 the old carbonyl carbon is one of the two end carboxyls of the new oxaloacetate (even odds for each end), and each turn removes both end carboxyls of the OAA it starts with.
cards.why: Combines the symmetry of succinate and fumarate (ends map to ends) with the rule that each turn removes the starting OAA's end carboxyls.
cards.quote: Each turn removes the two end carboxyls of the OAA it starts with
cards.section: Which carbons leave? A puzzle the net equation cannot answer

cards.front: Is O₂ a substrate of the citric acid cycle? Why is it still required?
cards.back: No. Oxygen appears in none of the eight reactions. It is needed only to empty the carriers via the ETC: required, but not a substrate.
cards.quote: Oxygen appears in none of the eight reactions; it is needed only to empty the carriers: required, but not a substrate.
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: Oxygen is cut off from respiring mitochondria. Which citric acid cycle steps stall first, and why does step 1 eventually slow too?
cards.back: The four dehydrogenases stall first: the small, fixed NAD⁺ pool fills as NADH, and step 6's FAD cannot empty into an already-full ubiquinone pool. With little OAA coming out of step 8, citrate synthase slows to a crawl.
cards.quote: Without O₂ the chain backs up and the small, fixed NAD⁺ pool fills up as NADH, leaving steps 3, 4 and 8 nothing to load.
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: Name the three main control points of the citric acid cycle.
cards.back: Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (the two irreversible oxidative decarboxylations), plus citrate synthase.
cards.quote: The best-known control points are the two irreversible oxidative decarboxylations, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: State the rule of thumb for which signals slow and which speed the citric acid cycle.
cards.back: ATP and NADH = STOP (the cell is rich, carriers full). ADP, NAD⁺ and Ca²⁺ = GO.
cards.quote: The rule: ATP and NADH = STOP (the cell is rich; high NADH means full carriers).
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: Give the two ways rising ADP speeds the citric acid cycle.
cards.back: It speeds the respiratory chain, so NAD⁺ comes back faster, and it directly activates isocitrate dehydrogenase.
cards.quote: Rising ADP speeds the respiratory chain, so NAD⁺ comes back faster, and ADP also activates isocitrate dehydrogenase directly.
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: How does mitochondrial Ca²⁺ in contracting muscle act on the citric acid cycle, and how does that differ from the ADP signal?
cards.back: Ca²⁺ is a push, not a gauge: it activates isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and (via PDH phosphatase) pyruvate dehydrogenase, raising NADH production the moment work starts.
cards.quote: Its main effect is not on emptying carriers: it raises NADH production the moment work starts.
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: A resting, well-fed cell has a high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio and a high ATP/ADP ratio. Predict flux through isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
cards.back: Slowed. High NADH and ATP are STOP signals; α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is also held back by its product NADH.
cards.quote: ADP, NAD⁺ and Ca²⁺ = GO (calcium works differently, below).
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: In a contracting muscle, mitochondrial Ca²⁺ rises but the oxygen supply is cut off. Will the Ca²⁺ signal keep the citric acid cycle running fast?
cards.back: No. Ca²⁺ activates the dehydrogenases, but each still needs an empty carrier; without O₂ the NAD⁺ pool fills as NADH and flux stalls.
cards.why: Rule: the cycle turns no faster than its carriers are emptied; Ca²⁺ raises NADH production, not carrier emptying.
cards.quote: Recall the guiding idea: the cycle turns no faster than its carriers are emptied.
cards.section: Oxygen and the throttle: one demand story

cards.front: Using the glycerol-phosphate shuttle (s = 1.5), with about 2.5 ATP per NADH and about 10 ATP per acetyl-CoA, total the ATP per glucose from 2 + 2 × 2.5 + 2 × 10 + 2 × s.
cards.back: 2 + 5 + 20 + 3 = 30 ATP per glucose. The 2 × 10 term is two acetyl-CoA through the cycle.
cards.section: Cash the carriers

cards.front: Switching from the glycerol-phosphate shuttle (s = 1.5) to the malate-aspartate shuttle (s = 2.5), what is the ATP yield per glucose, and why does it rise by exactly 2?
cards.back: 2 + 5 + 20 + 5 = 32 ATP. Only the shuttle term changes: 2 × 2.5 = 5 instead of 2 × 1.5 = 3.
cards.quote: Malate-aspartate shuttle (s = 2.5): 2 + 5 + 20 + 5 = 32 ATP per glucose.
cards.section: Cash the carriers

cards.front: What does it mean that the citric acid cycle is amphibolic?
cards.back: It serves both breakdown and building: citrate goes to fatty-acid synthesis, α-ketoglutarate to glutamate, succinyl-CoA to heme, OAA to gluconeogenesis.
cards.quote: The cycle is amphibolic: it serves both breakdown and building.
cards.section: Where the catalyst rule stops: amphibolic and anaplerotic

cards.front: In many tissues, which enzyme chiefly refills the citric acid cycle (anaplerosis), what reaction does it run, and what activates it?
cards.back: Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate + CO₂ → oxaloacetate. Activated by acetyl-CoA, a feedforward signal.
cards.quote: which adds CO₂ to pyruvate to make OAA and is switched on by acetyl-CoA, a feedforward signal
cards.section: Where the catalyst rule stops: amphibolic and anaplerotic

cards.front: A liver cell draws OAA off for gluconeogenesis while acetyl-CoA keeps arriving, but its pyruvate carboxylase is missing. Predict acetyl-CoA oxidation over time.
cards.back: Oxidation would be expected to slow: withdrawals shrink the OAA pool, citrate synthase is limited by OAA supply, and nothing refills it unless other anaplerotic sources do.
cards.why: Combines the amphibolic withdrawal rule with citrate synthase's dependence on OAA.
cards.quote: Each withdrawal takes carbon that would have become OAA, so the pool would shrink.
cards.section: Where the catalyst rule stops: amphibolic and anaplerotic

cards.front: A paraganglioma carries a loss-of-function mutation in succinate dehydrogenase. Which metabolite accumulates, and what role is it thought to play?
cards.back: Succinate piles up and acts as an oncometabolite.
cards.quote: Mutations in succinate dehydrogenase and fumarase let succinate and fumarate pile up as oncometabolites in paragangliomas and kidney cancer.
cards.section: Where the catalyst rule stops: amphibolic and anaplerotic

cards.front: A glioma has a gain-of-function IDH1 mutation that makes 2-hydroxyglutarate. Does step 3 of the citric acid cycle still run?
cards.back: Yes. Step 3 is run by the NAD⁺-dependent IDH3; mutant IDH1 or IDH2 are its NADP⁺-dependent cousins, and their product scrambles the epigenome.
cards.quote: Mutant IDH1 or IDH2, the NADP⁺-dependent cousins of the cycle's NAD⁺-dependent IDH3, gain a new activity
cards.section: Where the catalyst rule stops: amphibolic and anaplerotic

cards.front: Why is citrate synthase called the committed step of the citric acid cycle?
cards.back: It is one of the cycle's most exergonic steps (ΔG°′ ≈ −31.4 kJ/mol) and effectively irreversible, so it pulls the whole cycle forward.
cards.why: The citryl-CoA intermediate is hydrolyzed while still bound, so the thioester energy is not wasted.
cards.quote: The step is one of the cycle's most exergonic (ΔG°′ ≈ −31.4 kJ/mol) and effectively irreversible
cards.section: Citrate synthase's pull

cards.front: The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex shares pyruvate dehydrogenase's five cofactors. Name them.
cards.back: TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺.
cards.quote: its five cofactors (TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺) and its substrate channeling
cards.section: Pyruvate dehydrogenase's twin

cards.front: A {{c1::synthetase}}, unlike a synthase, uses or makes a nucleotide triphosphate.
cards.back: Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP (or ATP, depending on isoform); citrate synthase uses none.
cards.quote: A synthetase, unlike a synthase, uses or makes a nucleotide triphosphate.
cards.section: Synthase versus synthetase

cards.front: How does the Warburg effect rewire the entrance to the citric acid cycle?
cards.back: Tumors run glycolysis hard even with oxygen, turning more pyruvate into lactate rather than acetyl-CoA, though many keep a working cycle, often fed by glutamine.
cards.quote: more pyruvate is turned into lactate rather than entering the cycle as acetyl-CoA, although many tumors keep a working cycle
cards.section: The Warburg effect
